notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Water resources include all naturally available water that can be used by humans, ecosystems and economic activities.
  • Major sources include:
  • Rivers.
  • Lakes.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Groundwater.
  • Glaciers and snow.
  • Wetlands.
  • Rainwater.
  • Water is a renewable resource, but usable freshwater is limited and unevenly distributed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Resource → Renewable, but Limited and Uneven

2. Distribution of Water on Earth
  • Most of Earth's water is saline and occurs in oceans and seas.
  • Only a small fraction is freshwater.
  • Much freshwater is locked in glaciers, ice caps and groundwater.
  • Easily accessible freshwater in rivers and lakes forms only a very small part of the global water stock.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Earth has abundant water, but directly usable freshwater is limited.

3. Freshwater Sources in India
  • India's freshwater comes mainly from:
  • Monsoon rainfall.
  • Himalayan snow and glaciers.
  • Rivers.
  • Groundwater.
  • Lakes and reservoirs.
  • Wetlands.
4. Importance of Monsoon Rainfall
  • Monsoon rainfall is India's main source of freshwater recharge.
  • It replenishes:
  • Rivers.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Tanks.
  • Lakes.
  • Groundwater.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Weak monsoon years can therefore affect many water sources simultaneously.
5. Uneven Water Availability
  • Water availability varies because of differences in:
  • Rainfall.
  • River systems.
  • Geology.
  • Relief.
  • Population.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Storage capacity.
  • Some areas experience floods, while others face chronic water scarcity.
6. Seasonal Nature of Water Availability
  • A large share of India's rainfall occurs during a few monsoon months.
  • River flow is therefore strongly seasonal in many basins.
  • Storage structures are needed to conserve monsoon water for dry-season use.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India's Water Challenge → Seasonal Concentration of Rainfall

7. Surface Water
  • Surface water includes:
  • Rivers.
  • Streams.
  • Lakes.
  • Ponds.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Tanks.
  • Wetlands.
  • It is directly exposed to evaporation, pollution and seasonal fluctuations.
8. Groundwater
  • Groundwater is water stored below Earth's surface in pores, cracks and rock formations.
  • It is a major source of:
  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Rural domestic supply.
  • Urban water.
  • Excess extraction can cause serious depletion.
9. Water Table
  • Water table is the upper surface of the saturated groundwater zone.
  • It rises after recharge.
  • It falls when groundwater is extracted faster than it is replenished.
📌 Must-Memorise

Groundwater Upper Surface → Water Table

10. Zone of Saturation
  • Below the water table, pores and fractures are filled with water.
  • This region is called the zone of saturation.
11. Zone of Aeration
  • The zone above the water table contains both air and water in soil and rock pores.
  • It is also called the unsaturated zone.
12. Aquifer
  • An aquifer is a permeable geological formation capable of storing and transmitting groundwater.
  • Sand, gravel and fractured rocks can form productive aquifers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aquifer → Stores + Transmits Groundwater

13. Aquiclude
  • An aquiclude can store water but transmits it very slowly.
  • Clay-rich formations are common examples.
14. Aquitard
  • An aquitard transmits water more slowly than a good aquifer.
  • It can restrict groundwater movement.
15. Confined Aquifer
  • A confined aquifer lies between relatively impermeable layers.
  • Groundwater is under pressure.
  • A well penetrating it may show water rising above the top of the aquifer.
16. Unconfined Aquifer
  • An unconfined aquifer has no impermeable layer above it.
  • Its upper boundary is the water table.
  • It is directly recharged by infiltration from the surface.
17. Artesian Well
  • An artesian well taps a confined aquifer.
  • Pressure may cause water to rise naturally in the well.
  • In some cases, water may flow to the surface without pumping.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Artesian Well → Confined Aquifer + Pressure

18. Groundwater Recharge
  • Groundwater recharge occurs through:
  • Rainfall infiltration.
  • River seepage.
  • Tank and lake seepage.
  • Irrigation return flow.
  • Artificial recharge structures.
19. Infiltration
  • Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface into soil.
  • Permeable soil and vegetation promote infiltration.
  • Concrete surfaces reduce infiltration.
20. Percolation
  • Percolation is the downward movement of infiltrated water through soil and rock.
  • It helps recharge deeper groundwater.
21. Factors Affecting Groundwater Recharge
  • Recharge depends on:
  • Rainfall intensity.
  • Soil texture.
  • Rock permeability.
  • Vegetation.
  • Slope.
  • Land use.
  • Duration of rainfall.
22. Alluvial Aquifers
  • Northern Plains contain extensive alluvial aquifers.
  • Sand and gravel layers store large quantities of groundwater.
  • Tube-well irrigation is widespread.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plains → Major Alluvial Groundwater Aquifers

23. Hard-Rock Aquifers
  • Peninsular India contains large areas of hard crystalline rocks.
  • Groundwater occurs mainly in:
  • Weathered zones.
  • Joints.
  • Cracks.
  • Fractures.
  • Storage is generally more limited and localised than in thick alluvial aquifers.
24. Groundwater in Tamil Nadu
  • Much of Tamil Nadu contains hard-rock aquifers.
  • Groundwater availability varies considerably between districts.
  • Weathered and fractured crystalline rocks are important groundwater zones.
  • Coastal aquifers face risk of seawater intrusion.
25. Groundwater Over-Extraction
  • Excess groundwater extraction can cause:
  • Falling water table.
  • Dry wells.
  • Increased pumping cost.
  • Land subsidence in some areas.
  • Reduced baseflow to rivers.
  • Seawater intrusion in coastal areas.
26. Seawater Intrusion
  • Excessive extraction near the coast can lower freshwater pressure.
  • Seawater then moves into coastal aquifers.
  • Groundwater becomes saline.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coastal Over-Pumping → Seawater Intrusion

27. Groundwater Quality
  • Groundwater can be affected by:
  • Salinity.
  • Fluoride.
  • Arsenic.
  • Nitrate.
  • Iron.
  • Industrial pollution.
  • Sewage contamination.
28. Fluoride in Groundwater
  • Excess fluoride in drinking water can cause fluorosis.
  • Dental fluorosis affects teeth.
  • Skeletal fluorosis affects bones and joints.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Excess Fluoride → Fluorosis

29. Arsenic Contamination
  • Arsenic contamination is a serious groundwater issue in parts of the Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial plains.
  • Long-term exposure can cause serious health problems.
30. Nitrate Pollution
  • Nitrate can enter groundwater from:
  • Fertilisers.
  • Sewage.
  • Animal waste.
  • Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause methemoglobinemia, especially in infants.
31. Water Scarcity
  • Water scarcity occurs when:
  • Water demand exceeds available supply.
  • Water is physically unavailable.
  • Water quality makes available water unusable.
  • Infrastructure cannot deliver water effectively.
32. Physical Water Scarcity
  • Physical water scarcity occurs where naturally available water is insufficient to meet demand.
  • Arid and drought-prone regions are particularly vulnerable.
33. Economic Water Scarcity
  • Economic water scarcity occurs where water may exist but infrastructure, finance or institutions are inadequate to supply it.
34. Causes of Water Scarcity in India
  • Major causes include:
  • Uneven rainfall.
  • Population growth.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Irrigation demand.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • Pollution.
  • Poor storage.
  • Leakage and wastage.
  • Climate variability.
35. Agriculture and Water Use
  • Agriculture is India's largest water-consuming sector.
  • Irrigation accounts for a very large share of freshwater withdrawals.
  • Water-intensive crops increase pressure on water resources.
36. Irrigation
  • Irrigation means artificial supply of water to crops.
  • It supplements or replaces rainfall.
  • It is essential in areas with:
  • Low rainfall.
  • Uncertain rainfall.
  • Dry-season cultivation.
37. Major Sources of Irrigation
  • India uses:
  • Canals.
  • Wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Lift irrigation.
  • Micro-irrigation systems.
38. Canal Irrigation
  • Canals carry river or reservoir water to agricultural land.
  • Canal irrigation is important in the Northern Plains and major command areas.
39. Perennial Canal
  • A perennial canal receives regulated water throughout much of the year from a permanent river or reservoir.
40. Inundation Canal
  • Inundation canals draw water during periods of high river flow.
  • They traditionally function mainly during flood seasons.
41. Well Irrigation
  • Wells tap shallow groundwater.
  • They are widely used in alluvial and hard-rock regions where groundwater is accessible.
42. Tube Wells
  • Tube wells tap groundwater through drilled pipes.
  • Pumping allows large quantities of water to be extracted.
  • They are particularly common in northern alluvial plains.
43. Tank Irrigation
  • Tanks store rainwater and surface runoff.
  • Tank irrigation is historically important in peninsular India.
  • Tamil Nadu has an extensive traditional tank system.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Traditional Irrigation Strength → Tanks

44. Why Tanks Are Important in Peninsular India
  • Reasons include:
  • Undulating terrain.
  • Seasonal rivers.
  • Hard-rock geology.
  • Natural depressions.
  • Seasonal concentration of rainfall.
45. Tamil Nadu Tank Irrigation
  • Tanks collect monsoon runoff.
  • They support agriculture in areas without reliable perennial rivers.
  • Many are interconnected in cascades.
  • They also recharge groundwater.
46. Eri System
  • Traditional irrigation tanks in Tamil Nadu are commonly called eri.
  • Eri systems store rainfall and river runoff.
  • They have long supported paddy cultivation and village water management.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Traditional Tank → Eri

47. Cascade Tank System
  • A series of tanks may be connected so that overflow from an upper tank enters a lower tank.
  • This improves water use and groundwater recharge.
48. Lift Irrigation
  • Lift irrigation raises water from a lower level to higher agricultural land using pumps.
  • It is useful where gravity flow is not possible.
49. Micro-Irrigation
  • Micro-irrigation includes:
  • Drip irrigation.
  • Sprinkler irrigation.
  • These systems aim to improve water-use efficiency.
50. Drip Irrigation
  • Drip irrigation delivers water directly near plant roots.
  • Water is supplied in small quantities through pipes and emitters.
  • Evaporation and conveyance losses are reduced.
📌 Must-Memorise

Drip → Water Near Root Zone

51. Crops Suitable for Drip Irrigation
  • Drip irrigation is useful for:
  • Fruit crops.
  • Vegetables.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Cotton.
  • Plantation crops.
52. Sprinkler Irrigation
  • Sprinkler irrigation distributes water through pressurised pipes and nozzles.
  • Water falls over crops like artificial rain.
  • It is useful on uneven land and sandy soils.
53. Drip vs Sprinkler
  • Drip:
  • Root-zone application.
  • Very high efficiency.
  • Best for widely spaced crops.
  • Sprinkler:
  • Sprays over field.
  • Useful on uneven land.
  • Suitable for many field crops.
54. Flood Irrigation
  • Water is allowed to flow over fields.
  • It is simple but may have high losses from:
  • Evaporation.
  • Runoff.
  • Deep percolation.
  • Poorly managed flood irrigation can cause waterlogging and salinity.
55. Waterlogging
  • Waterlogging occurs when the water table rises close to the soil surface.
  • Soil pores become filled with water.
  • Root aeration decreases.
  • Crop productivity can decline.
56. Soil Salinity from Irrigation
  • Excess irrigation in poorly drained areas can raise the water table.
  • Evaporation leaves salts near the surface.
  • This may reduce agricultural productivity.
57. Irrigation Efficiency
  • Irrigation efficiency refers to the proportion of supplied water effectively used by crops.
  • Improving efficiency reduces unnecessary withdrawals.
58. Multipurpose River Valley Projects
  • Multipurpose projects may provide:
  • Irrigation.
  • Hydroelectric power.
  • Flood control.
  • Drinking water.
  • Industrial water.
  • Navigation.
  • Fisheries.
  • Recreation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Multipurpose Dam → Many Uses from One Project

59. Dam
  • A dam is a barrier constructed across a river or valley.
  • It stores or controls water.
  • Water stored behind a dam forms a reservoir.
60. Reservoir
  • A reservoir is an artificial or enlarged water body created mainly for storage.
  • It can regulate highly seasonal river flow.
61. Major Benefits of Dams
  • Benefits include:
  • Irrigation.
  • Electricity.
  • Water supply.
  • Flood moderation.
  • Drought relief.
  • Fisheries.
62. Major Problems Associated with Large Dams
  • Potential problems include:
  • Displacement of people.
  • Forest submergence.
  • Habitat loss.
  • Sediment trapping.
  • Changes in downstream flow.
  • Rehabilitation issues.
  • Altered fish migration.
63. Sedimentation of Reservoirs
  • Rivers carry sediment into reservoirs.
  • Sediment gradually accumulates.
  • This reduces storage capacity.
  • Catchment erosion accelerates sedimentation.
64. Catchment Area
  • A catchment or drainage basin is the area from which water drains into a river, lake or reservoir.
  • Catchment management affects both water quantity and quality.
65. Watershed
  • A watershed is a land area that drains to a common outlet.
  • In Indian development programmes, watershed often refers to a small drainage catchment managed as a unit.
66. Watershed Management
  • Watershed management aims to:
  • Reduce soil erosion.
  • Increase infiltration.
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Slow surface runoff.
  • Improve vegetation.
  • Enhance water availability.
67. Contour Bunding
  • Bunds are constructed along contour lines.
  • They slow runoff.
  • They reduce soil erosion.
  • They increase infiltration.
68. Check Dam
  • A check dam is a small barrier across a stream or drainage channel.
  • It slows runoff.
  • Water temporarily collects behind it.
  • Groundwater recharge can increase.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Check Dam → Slow Runoff + Recharge Groundwater

69. Percolation Pond
  • A percolation pond stores runoff in a shallow depression.
  • Stored water infiltrates gradually.
  • Its main purpose is groundwater recharge.
70. Recharge Well
  • Recharge wells direct surface water into deeper permeable formations.
  • They are used where natural infiltration is limited.
71. Rainwater Harvesting
  • Rainwater harvesting means collecting and storing rainwater or directing it for groundwater recharge.
  • It reduces dependence on external water supplies.
72. Rooftop Rainwater Harvesting
  • Typical system includes:
  • Roof catchment.
  • Gutters.
  • Downpipe.
  • Filter.
  • Storage tank or recharge structure.
73. Benefits of Rainwater Harvesting
  • Increases local water availability.
  • Recharges groundwater.
  • Reduces storm runoff.
  • Reduces urban flooding.
  • Supplements domestic supply.
74. Tamil Nadu and Rainwater Harvesting
  • Rainwater harvesting is particularly important in Tamil Nadu because rainfall is seasonal and groundwater pressure is high.
  • Rooftop recharge systems are widely promoted in both urban and rural areas.
75. Traditional Water Harvesting Systems in India
  • Examples include:
  • Johads.
  • Tankas.
  • Khadins.
  • Baolis/stepwells.
  • Ahars and pynes.
  • Eris.
  • Kulhs.
76. Johad
  • Johads are small earthen water-harvesting structures traditionally used in Rajasthan.
  • They collect runoff and improve groundwater recharge.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Johad → Rajasthan

77. Tanka
  • Tanka is an underground or covered rainwater-storage structure.
  • It is traditionally used in arid Rajasthan.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tanka → Rajasthan Rainwater Storage

78. Khadin
  • Khadin is a traditional runoff-harvesting system of Rajasthan.
  • Water is impounded behind an earthen embankment.
  • Moisture retained in soil supports crop cultivation.
79. Baoli / Stepwell
  • Stepwells are deep wells accessed by steps.
  • They were historically important in western and northern India.
  • They stored groundwater and provided public water access.
80. Ahar-Pyne System
  • Ahar-Pyne is a traditional water-management system associated mainly with Bihar.
  • Ahars are storage structures.
  • Pynes are channels that carry water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ahar-Pyne → Bihar

81. Kulh
  • Kulhs are traditional water channels used in Himalayan regions, particularly Himachal Pradesh.
  • They divert mountain-stream water for irrigation.
82. Eri
  • Eris are traditional irrigation tanks of Tamil Nadu.
  • They store monsoon runoff.
  • They are highly important for local irrigation and groundwater recharge.
83. Urban Water Supply
  • Urban water commonly comes from:
  • Reservoirs.
  • Rivers.
  • Groundwater.
  • Lakes.
  • Long-distance pipelines.
  • Desalination in some coastal cities.
84. Chennai Water Sources — Geography Link
  • Chennai depends on a combination of:
  • Reservoirs.
  • Groundwater.
  • Inter-basin transfers.
  • Desalination.
  • Monsoon-fed lakes and tanks.
85. Desalination
  • Desalination removes dissolved salts from seawater or brackish water.
  • It provides freshwater in water-scarce coastal regions.
  • Reverse osmosis is a commonly used technology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Desalination → Seawater to Freshwater

86. Reverse Osmosis
  • Reverse osmosis uses pressure to force water through a semi-permeable membrane.
  • Salts and many impurities are separated from the water.
87. Desalination Limitations
  • Challenges include:
  • High energy use.
  • High cost.
  • Brine disposal.
  • Marine environmental impacts.
88. Water Pollution
  • Water pollution occurs when harmful substances degrade water quality.
  • Major sources include:
  • Sewage.
  • Industrial effluents.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Solid waste.
  • Oil.
  • Mining wastes.
89. Sewage Pollution
  • Untreated sewage adds organic matter and pathogens to water.
  • Decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen.
  • Waterborne diseases can spread.
90. Industrial Water Pollution
  • Industries may release:
  • Heavy metals.
  • Acids.
  • Alkalis.
  • Dyes.
  • Organic chemicals.
  • Heated water.
  • Treatment is needed before discharge.
91. Agricultural Runoff
  • Fertilisers and pesticides can wash into rivers and lakes.
  • Nitrogen and phosphorus promote eutrophication.
  • Pesticides may affect aquatic organisms.
92. Eutrophication
  • Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water.
  • Excess nitrogen and phosphorus stimulate algal growth.
  • Decomposition can reduce dissolved oxygen.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nutrients ↑ → Algal Bloom → Oxygen ↓

93. Biological Oxygen Demand
  • BOD means Biological Oxygen Demand.
  • It indicates the oxygen needed by microorganisms to decompose biodegradable organic matter.
  • High BOD generally indicates greater organic pollution.
📌 Must-Memorise

High BOD → High Organic Pollution

94. Dissolved Oxygen
  • Dissolved oxygen, or DO, is oxygen present in water.
  • Fish and many other aquatic organisms require it.
  • Severe organic pollution can reduce DO.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Clean Water → Generally Higher DO
Organic Pollution → Higher BOD, Lower DO

95. Chemical Oxygen Demand
  • COD measures oxygen equivalent required to chemically oxidise pollutants.
  • It is another indicator of water pollution.
96. Thermal Pollution
  • Discharge of hot water raises water temperature.
  • Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen.
  • Aquatic ecosystems may be affected.
97. Groundwater Pollution
  • Groundwater pollution is difficult to reverse because:
  • Water moves slowly underground.
  • Pollutants may remain for long periods.
  • Aquifer cleaning is costly.
98. River Pollution
  • Major causes include:
  • Urban sewage.
  • Industrial discharge.
  • Religious and domestic waste.
  • Agricultural runoff.
  • Solid-waste dumping.
99. Wetlands as Water Resources
  • Wetlands:
  • Store water.
  • Reduce floods.
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Filter pollutants.
  • Support biodiversity.
100. Floodplain Wetlands
  • Floodplain wetlands store excess river water.
  • They can reduce downstream flood peaks.
  • Encroachment reduces this natural storage function.
101. Lakes
  • Lakes may be:
  • Freshwater.
  • Saline.
  • Natural.
  • Artificial.
  • Tectonic.
  • Glacial.
  • Lagoonal.
102. Important Freshwater Lakes
  • Examples include:
  • Wular.
  • Loktak.
  • Kolleru.
  • Different lakes have different geological origins.
103. Wular Lake
  • Wular Lake lies in Jammu and Kashmir.
  • It is an important freshwater lake.
  • It is associated with the Jhelum River system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wular → Jammu & Kashmir

104. Loktak Lake
  • Loktak Lake lies in Manipur.
  • It is famous for floating masses of vegetation and organic matter called phumdis.
  • Keibul Lamjao National Park is located on floating phumdi formations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Loktak → Manipur → Phumdis

105. Kolleru Lake
  • Kolleru lies in Andhra Pradesh.
  • It is a freshwater lake between the Krishna and Godavari delta regions.
106. Saline and Brackish Lakes
  • Examples include:
  • Sambhar → Inland saline lake.
  • Chilika → Brackish lagoon.
  • Pulicat → Brackish lagoon.
107. Reservoirs
  • Important reservoirs are associated with major dams across:
  • Himalayan rivers.
  • Peninsular rivers.
  • Central Indian rivers.
  • Detailed project-by-project facts will be integrated with river chapters.
108. Inter-Basin Water Transfer
  • Inter-basin transfer means moving water from one river basin to another.
  • It aims to address regional imbalance in water availability.
  • Such projects involve significant engineering, ecological and social considerations.
109. River Interlinking — Concept
  • River interlinking proposes connecting selected river basins through canals and reservoirs.
  • Intended purposes include:
  • Irrigation.
  • Water transfer.
  • Flood moderation.
  • Drought relief.
  • Potential ecological and displacement impacts require careful assessment.
110. Water Conservation
  • Major conservation methods include:
  • Rainwater harvesting.
  • Watershed management.
  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Tank restoration.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Reuse of treated wastewater.
  • Leakage reduction.
111. Demand-Side Management
  • Water conservation is not only about increasing supply.
  • Demand can be reduced through:
  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Low-water crops.
  • Reuse.
  • Metering.
  • Leakage control.
  • Water-saving household devices.
112. Wastewater Reuse
  • Treated wastewater can be reused for:
  • Industry.
  • Landscaping.
  • Agriculture in suitable conditions.
  • Non-potable urban uses.
  • Reuse reduces demand for freshwater.
113. Greywater
  • Greywater is relatively less contaminated household wastewater from baths, sinks and laundry.
  • After suitable treatment, it can be reused for some non-potable purposes.
114. Blackwater
  • Blackwater contains toilet waste.
  • It requires more intensive treatment because of pathogens and high organic load.
115. Water Footprint
  • Water footprint represents freshwater used directly and indirectly to produce goods or services.
  • Food products can have large indirect water requirements.
116. Virtual Water
  • Virtual water is water embedded in the production of a commodity.
  • When a water-intensive product is traded, virtual water is effectively transferred between regions.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Virtual Water → Hidden Water Used in Production

117. Water-Intensive Crops
  • Examples include:
  • Paddy.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Their impact depends on local climate, irrigation efficiency and water availability.
118. Crop Choice and Water Conservation
  • Matching crops to local rainfall and water availability can reduce irrigation stress.
  • Millets generally require less water than paddy or sugarcane.
119. Drought-Proofing
  • Measures include:
  • Watershed development.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Tank restoration.
  • Drought-resistant crops.
  • Micro-irrigation.
  • Groundwater recharge.
120. Farm Pond
  • A farm pond is a small water-storage structure on agricultural land.
  • It captures runoff for supplementary irrigation.
121. Check Dam vs Large Dam
  • Check dam:
  • Small.
  • Local.
  • Mainly slows runoff and improves recharge.
  • Large dam:
  • Major storage.
  • Multipurpose uses.
  • Larger environmental and social impacts.
122. Watershed vs River Basin
  • A river basin is the full land area drained by a river and its tributaries.
  • A watershed can refer to a smaller drainage unit within a larger basin.
  • Both are bounded by drainage divides.
123. Drainage Divide
  • A drainage divide is elevated land separating neighbouring drainage basins.
  • Water falling on opposite sides flows to different river systems.
124. Perennial River
  • A perennial river carries water throughout the year.
  • Himalayan rivers are generally perennial because they receive rainfall plus snow/glacier melt.
125. Seasonal River
  • Seasonal rivers carry much more water during rainy periods.
  • Many peninsular rivers show greater seasonal variation than Himalayan rivers.
126. Baseflow
  • Baseflow is groundwater contribution to river flow.
  • Excess groundwater extraction can reduce river flow during dry periods.
127. Surface Runoff
  • Runoff is water flowing over land into streams and rivers.
  • Urbanisation generally increases rapid runoff because paved surfaces reduce infiltration.
128. Urbanisation and Water Cycle
  • Urbanisation can cause:
  • Less infiltration.
  • More runoff.
  • More flooding.
  • Lower groundwater recharge.
  • Increased water demand.
129. Wetland Encroachment
  • Filling or building over wetlands reduces natural water storage.
  • This can increase urban flood risk.
  • It also reduces groundwater recharge and biodiversity.
130. Chennai — Water Geography
  • Important geographical issues include:
  • Seasonal rainfall concentration.
  • Dependence on northeast monsoon.
  • Coastal groundwater stress.
  • Urban lake and wetland management.
  • Flood-drought cycles.
131. Tamil Nadu and Seasonal Water Scarcity
  • Tamil Nadu has limited major perennial rivers originating entirely within the state.
  • Rainfall is strongly seasonal.
  • Therefore, reservoirs, tanks and groundwater are especially important.
132. Tamil Nadu River Dependence
  • Tamil Nadu depends on:
  • Kaveri system.
  • Tamiraparani.
  • Vaigai.
  • Palar.
  • Pennaiyar.
  • Numerous smaller rivers and tanks.
  • Detailed river facts will be covered later.
133. Tamiraparani — Water Resource Link
  • Tamiraparani is an important river of southern Tamil Nadu.
  • It is relatively dependable compared with many seasonal rivers because its catchment receives substantial rainfall from the Western Ghats.
134. Kaveri — Water Resource Link
  • Kaveri is one of Tamil Nadu's most important rivers.
  • It supports:
  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Agriculture.
  • Hydropower.
  • Its delta is a major rice-growing region.
135. Palar — Water Resource Link
  • Palar is a highly seasonal river.
  • Groundwater extraction in its basin is important for local water supply.
136. Vaigai — Water Resource Link
  • Vaigai supports irrigation and water supply in southern Tamil Nadu.
  • It is associated with the Vaigai reservoir system.
137. Water and Agriculture in Tamil Nadu
  • Major issues include:
  • Dependence on monsoon.
  • Tank irrigation.
  • Groundwater extraction.
  • Delta irrigation.
  • Drought risk.
  • Salinity in coastal areas.
138. Tank Restoration
  • Restoring tanks can:
  • Increase storage.
  • Improve irrigation.
  • Recharge wells.
  • Reduce local flooding.
  • Support wetland biodiversity.
139. Desilting
  • Desilting removes accumulated sediment from tanks, canals or reservoirs.
  • It can restore storage capacity.
  • Catchment erosion must also be controlled to prevent rapid re-siltation.
140. Evaporation Loss
  • Open reservoirs lose water through evaporation.
  • Evaporation is particularly high in hot and dry regions.
141. Water Conservation in Agriculture
  • Methods include:
  • Drip irrigation.
  • Sprinklers.
  • Mulching.
  • Proper irrigation timing.
  • Laser land levelling.
  • Drought-resistant crops.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.
142. Mulching
  • Mulch covers the soil surface.
  • It reduces evaporation.
  • It suppresses weeds.
  • It can conserve soil moisture.
143. Water Harvesting and Flood Control
  • Rainwater harvesting can:
  • Capture local runoff.
  • Reduce pressure on storm drains.
  • Lower flood peaks.
  • Recharge groundwater.
144. Water Security
  • Water security means reliable access to sufficient water of acceptable quality for:
  • Human health.
  • Livelihoods.
  • Economic activity.
  • Ecosystems.
145. Water Stress
  • Water stress occurs when demand approaches or exceeds renewable water availability or when quality limits usable supply.
  • High population density and irrigation demand can increase stress.
146. Water Conservation Hierarchy
  • A practical approach is:
  • Reduce wastage.
  • Improve efficiency.
  • Reuse water.
  • Recharge local sources.
  • Develop new supplies only where necessary.
147. Important Water Terms
  • Aquifer → Groundwater-bearing formation.
  • Recharge → Replenishment of groundwater.
  • Watershed → Drainage unit.
  • Runoff → Surface flow.
  • Infiltration → Entry into soil.
  • Percolation → Downward movement.
  • Reservoir → Stored surface water.
  • Water table → Top of saturated groundwater.
148. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Aquifer → Groundwater.
  • Water table → Saturated-zone upper boundary.
  • Artesian → Confined aquifer.
  • Eri → Tamil Nadu tank.
  • Johad → Rajasthan.
  • Tanka → Rajasthan.
  • Khadin → Rajasthan.
  • Ahar-Pyne → Bihar.
  • Kulh → Himachal Pradesh.
  • Drip → Root zone.
  • Sprinkler → Artificial rainfall.
  • Check dam → Recharge.
  • Percolation pond → Recharge.
  • BOD → Organic pollution.
  • DO → Aquatic oxygen.
  • Eutrophication → Nutrient enrichment.
  • Loktak → Phumdis.
  • Sambhar → Saline.
  • Chilika → Brackish.
  • Kolleru → Freshwater.
  • Desalination → Salt removal.
149. TNPSC Traps
  • Renewable water does not mean unlimited water.
  • Groundwater is not an underground river everywhere.
  • Aquifer stores and transmits groundwater.
  • Water table is not fixed; it rises and falls.
  • Northern alluvial plains generally have better groundwater storage than hard-rock plateaus.
  • Over-pumping can cause seawater intrusion in coastal areas.
  • Tank irrigation is highly important in peninsular India.
  • Tamil Nadu traditional tanks are called eris.
  • Drip irrigation does not spray the whole field.
  • Sprinkler irrigation resembles artificial rain.
  • Excess irrigation can cause both waterlogging and salinity.
  • Check dams mainly slow runoff and increase recharge; they are not equivalent to large reservoirs.
  • Rainwater harvesting can involve storage or recharge.
  • High BOD indicates greater organic pollution.
  • High DO is generally favourable to aquatic life.
  • Eutrophication is mainly linked to nitrogen and phosphorus enrichment.
  • Loktak is famous for phumdis.
  • Kolleru is freshwater.
  • Chilika and Pulicat are brackish.
  • Desalination provides freshwater but requires energy.
  • Reservoir sedimentation reduces storage.
  • Wetlands reduce flood risk by storing water.
  • Groundwater depletion can reduce dry-season river baseflow.
  • Urban paving increases runoff and reduces recharge.
  • Water scarcity can result from poor quality even when water quantity appears adequate.
150. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Water → Uneven.
  • Monsoon → Main recharge.
  • Surface → River/lake.
  • Groundwater → Aquifer.
  • Water table → Saturation top.
  • Recharge → Infiltration.
  • North plains → Alluvial aquifers.
  • Peninsula → Hard rock.
  • Coast → Saline intrusion risk.
  • Irrigation → Agriculture.
  • Canal → River/reservoir.
  • Tube well → Groundwater.
  • Tank → Peninsular.
  • Eri → Tamil Nadu.
  • Drip → Roots.
  • Sprinkler → Spray.
  • Dam → Storage.
  • Check dam → Recharge.
  • Johad → Rajasthan.
  • Tanka → Rajasthan.
  • Ahar-Pyne → Bihar.
  • Kulh → Himachal.
  • BOD high → Pollution high.
  • DO high → Better water.
  • Loktak → Phumdi.
  • Desalination → Sea to fresh.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Main source of India's freshwater recharge? → Monsoon rainfall.
  • What is surface water? → Water in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, tanks and wetlands.
  • What is groundwater? → Water stored below Earth's surface.
  • Upper surface of groundwater saturation zone? → Water table.
  • What is an aquifer? → Permeable formation that stores and transmits groundwater.
  • What is a confined aquifer? → Aquifer bounded by less permeable layers and under pressure.
  • What is an unconfined aquifer? → Aquifer whose upper surface is the water table.
  • What is an artesian well? → Well tapping a pressurised confined aquifer.
  • What is infiltration? → Movement of surface water into soil.
  • What is percolation? → Downward movement of water through soil and rock.
  • Which region has major alluvial aquifers? → Northern Plains.
  • How is groundwater commonly stored in hard-rock peninsular regions? → Weathered and fractured rocks.
  • Major danger of excessive coastal groundwater pumping? → Seawater intrusion.
  • Excess fluoride causes? → Fluorosis.
  • Groundwater arsenic problem is especially associated with? → Parts of Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial plains.
  • Nitrate contamination may come from? → Fertilisers and sewage.
  • Largest water-consuming sector in India? → Agriculture.
  • What is irrigation? → Artificial supply of water to crops.
  • Main irrigation sources? → Canals, wells, tube wells, tanks and reservoirs.
  • Traditional tank irrigation is especially important in? → Peninsular India.
  • Traditional Tamil Nadu tank called? → Eri.
  • Main benefit of tank cascades? → Store runoff and recharge groundwater.
  • What is lift irrigation? → Pumping water from lower to higher land.
  • What is drip irrigation? → Water supplied directly near roots.
  • What is sprinkler irrigation? → Water sprayed like rainfall.
  • Which irrigation method generally saves more water for widely spaced crops? → Drip irrigation.
  • Possible effects of excessive irrigation? → Waterlogging and salinity.
  • What is a dam? → Barrier built across a river or valley to control/store water.
  • Water body formed behind a dam? → Reservoir.
  • Uses of multipurpose projects? → Irrigation, power, water supply, flood control and other uses.
  • Main long-term problem reducing reservoir capacity? → Sedimentation.
  • What is a watershed? → Land area draining to a common outlet.
  • Main objective of watershed management? → Conserve soil and water and improve recharge.
  • What is a check dam? → Small barrier slowing runoff and increasing recharge.
  • Purpose of percolation pond? → Groundwater recharge.
  • What is rainwater harvesting? → Collection, storage or recharge of rainwater.
  • Traditional Rajasthan runoff structure? → Johad.
  • Traditional underground Rajasthan rainwater store? → Tanka.
  • Traditional Rajasthan farming water system using embankments? → Khadin.
  • Ahar-Pyne belongs to? → Bihar.
  • Kulh belongs mainly to? → Himachal Pradesh.
  • Eri belongs to? → Tamil Nadu.
  • What is desalination? → Removal of salts from saline water.
  • Common desalination method? → Reverse osmosis.
  • Major disadvantage of desalination? → High energy use and brine disposal.
  • What is eutrophication? → Nutrient enrichment causing excessive algal growth.
  • Main nutrients causing eutrophication? → Nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • BOD full form? → Biological Oxygen Demand.
  • High BOD indicates? → Greater organic pollution.
  • DO full form? → Dissolved Oxygen.
  • What usually happens to DO during severe organic pollution? → It decreases.
  • What is COD? → Chemical Oxygen Demand.
  • What is thermal pollution? → Harmful warming of water by heated discharge.
  • What is greywater? → Wastewater from baths, sinks and laundry excluding toilet waste.
  • What is blackwater? → Wastewater containing toilet waste.
  • What is virtual water? → Water used indirectly to produce a commodity.
  • Major water-intensive crops? → Paddy and sugarcane.
  • Which crops generally require less water than paddy? → Millets.
  • Famous Manipur lake with floating phumdis? → Loktak Lake.
  • Wular Lake lies in? → Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Kolleru Lake lies in? → Andhra Pradesh.
  • Sambhar Lake is? → Saline.
  • Chilika Lake is? → Brackish lagoon.
  • Why are wetlands important for water management? → They store floodwater, recharge groundwater and filter pollutants.
  • What is baseflow? → Groundwater contribution to river flow.
  • What happens to infiltration with extensive urban paving? → It decreases.
  • What happens to runoff with extensive paving? → It increases.
  • Important traditional water-storage system for Tamil Nadu agriculture? → Tanks/eris.
  • Why is rainwater harvesting particularly important in Tamil Nadu? → Seasonal rainfall and high groundwater dependence.
  • What is water security? → Reliable access to adequate, safe water for people, economy and ecosystems.
